papers.title: Interpretable competing-risk prediction of hepatocellular carcinoma in cirrhosis from region-wide routine health data
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.26368516 v1

summary.one_liner: A three-class, interpretable Explainable Boosting Machine trained on one year of routine electronic health records predicts 12-month hepatocellular carcinoma (liver cancer) in cirrhosis while separating competing deaths and liver transplants, and outperformed aMAP and the Toronto HCC Risk Index in a region-wide Andalusian cohort.
summary.plain: Some people with cirrhosis (scarring of the liver) develop liver cancer, but others die or receive a transplant first, which makes predicting cancer harder. The researchers built a transparent computer model using a year of routine health records from a region of Spain, and asked it to sort each patient's next year into liver cancer, death or transplant without cancer, or neither. It predicted liver cancer better than two established risk scores, and it showed whether each abnormal test result pointed toward cancer or toward liver failure.
summary.why: Earlier risk scores ignore the chance that a patient dies of liver disease before cancer appears, which can mislead decisions about who needs closer surveillance. The text reports better discrimination and fewer competing deaths in the high-risk group, but these are retrospective analyses of one regional database, so whether this improves patient care in practice is untested here.
summary.background:
- Cirrhosis: late-stage scarring of the liver, a major risk factor for liver cancer (hepatocellular carcinoma, HCC).
- Competing risk: when another event (such as death from liver failure) can stop the outcome of interest from happening, so it must be modelled separately.
- AUROC / concordance: a 0 to 1 score of how well a model ranks patients who will have an event above those who will not; 0.5 is chance.
- aMAP and Toronto HCC Risk Index: existing clinical scores that estimate liver cancer risk.
- Explainable Boosting Machine: a machine-learning method built from simple per-variable curves, so each input's effect can be read directly.
- Cross-validation: testing a model repeatedly on held-out subsets of the data to estimate how it will generalise.
- Routine health data: records collected during normal care, such as diagnoses and blood tests, not data from a trial.

papers.abstract: Background. Short-term prediction of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in cirrhosis is complicated by the competing risk of death from liver disease. We aimed to develop an interpretable model on region-wide routine data that predicts HCC while separating competing mortality, and to compare it with established risk scores. Methods. From a region-wide cohort of adults with cirrhosis in the Andalusian Population Health Database, we trained the model on 17,177 patients with a prediction date set 12 months before their outcome, between 2020 and 2023. From one year of electronic health records before that date (demographics, liver and chronic disease codes, and eight routine laboratory tests), an Explainable Boosting Machine without interaction terms classified the following 12 months as HCC, death or liver transplantation without HCC, or event-free. We evaluated it in 20 repeats of 5-fold cross-validation against a binary model, a model with pair interactions and a model using the full health record, all on the same folds. We then applied the cross-validated models, without retraining, at the first routine encounter at which aMAP or the Toronto HCC Risk Index could be computed, and compared them with the scores in patients followed forward under competing risks, with and without a 6-month washout and with each province left out of training in turn. Findings. 771 patients (4.5%) developed HCC within 12 months and 3,314 (19.3%) died or underwent liver transplantation without HCC (3,061 deaths, 253 transplants). In cross-validation, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) for HCC was 0.734 (SD 0.018). A binary formulation, pairwise interactions and the full health record (more than 3,000 features) did not improve it; the full record lowered it by 0.024. At routine encounters the model discriminated 12-month HCC better than aMAP (time-dependent AUC 0.790 vs 0.688; difference +0.102, 95% CI +0.071 to +0.132) and the Toronto HCC Risk Index (0.761 vs 0.703; +0.057, +0.032 to +0.081), and remained better after excluding HCC diagnosed within 6 months (concordance difference +0.055 and +0.040) and when each of the eight provinces was left out of training. At equal group size, its high-risk group held as much HCC as the scores' high-risk categories, with 20-28% fewer competing deaths. Its shape functions separated cancer-specific signal (AFP rising from 2 to 20 g/L, platelets below 150 x10^9/L) from liver failure (bilirubin above 51 mol/L, albumin below 35 g/L); a binary model showed only the first. Interpretation. An interpretable three-class model on routine data outperformed established scores for short-term HCC risk in cirrhosis, while showing whether each abnormal value points to cancer or to competing death.

papers.title: Unified Machine Learning Model for Early Detection of Mild Cognitive Impairment, Frailty, and Fall Risk Using Multimodal Motor-Function Data
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.26368462 v1

summary.one_liner: A small study (n=79 community-dwelling older adults) trains a single multi-label machine learning model on sensor-based motor tests to predict mild cognitive impairment, frailty, and fall risk together, and compares it with separate single-condition models.
summary.plain: Older adults often have memory decline, physical frailty, and a higher risk of falls at the same time, and these conditions are usually screened separately. This study tested whether one computer model could estimate all three from a single set of movement tests (walking, standing up from a chair, balance, stepping, and reaction time) recorded with sensors. The unified model did about as well as three separate models, with the best accuracy for memory impairment and weaker accuracy for frailty and fall risk.
summary.why: The idea of screening several age-related conditions from one short assessment could make checkups more efficient if it holds up. The authors are measured about this: the sample is small, the model overestimated risk for all three outcomes, and fall-risk prediction was weak, so it needs recalibration and testing in other groups before any practical use.
summary.background:
- Mild cognitive impairment (MCI): noticeable memory or thinking decline that is not severe enough to be dementia.
- Frailty: a state of physical weakness and reduced reserve that raises vulnerability to health problems.
- Fall risk: the likelihood that a person will fall, often judged from balance and gait.
- Machine learning classifier: a model that learns from example data to sort people into groups (here, at risk or not).
- Multi-label classification: predicting several yes/no conditions at once for the same person.
- AUC (area under the ROC curve): a 0.5 score is chance and 1.0 is perfect separation of cases from non-cases; here the overall score of 0.645 is modest.
- Cross-validation: testing a model on data held out from training, repeated to estimate reliability.
- SHAP: a method that shows how much each input feature pushes a prediction up or down.
- Dual-task testing: performing a movement while doing a second mental task, which often reveals hidden problems.

papers.abstract: Background: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI), frailty, and fall risk often co-occur in older adults and share motor signs, yet they are screened and modeled separately. A unified model that predicts all 3 conditions from 1 sensor-based assessment could support earlier and more efficient screening, but such a model has rarely been developed or rigorously compared with separate models. Objective: This study aimed to develop a unified machine learning model that predicts MCI, frailty, and fall risk together from sensor-based motor-function data, compare it with separate single-label models, explain its predictions, and test its robustness. Methods: Community-dwelling older adults (n=79) completed a multimodal motor-function assessment with the Mizzou Point-of-Care Assessment System (MPASS), covering gait, sit-to-stand, static balance, step-down, and reaction time, with some tasks repeated under a dual-task condition. With demographic and family-history data, this yielded 59 features. Unified classifier-chain and single-label models were built with 5 algorithms across 6 modeling stages, evaluated with repeated nested cross-validation, and compared using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and paired bootstrap tests. The final model was explained with Shapley additive explanations (SHAP), and its robustness and the sufficiency of the sample size were tested with chain-input, chain-order sensitivity, domain-ablation, learning-curve, and power analyses. Results: With class weighting, the unified model had a higher mean AUC than the single-label models in 17 of 20 configurations and was never significantly worse, and it performed at least as well under nested model selection (0.615 vs 0.605; P=.58). The final extra trees model achieved a mean AUC of 0.645 (95% CI 0.569-0.722); discrimination was best for MCI (AUC 0.779, 95% CI 0.680-0.872) and lower for frailty (0.606) and fall risk (0.551). The model overestimated risk for all 3 outcomes, most for frailty. Most features (43/59, 73%), led by stride length, were shared across the 3 conditions, with consistent SHAP rankings in training and test participants ({rho}=0.99). Predicted frailty was the most important input for fall risk, and the 45 sensor features alone performed as well as the full model. Learning curves suggested that fall-risk prediction would benefit from more participants. Conclusions: A unified model predicted MCI, frailty, and fall risk together from one sensor-based assessment and performed as well as 3 separate models. It identified motor features shared across the conditions and used the link between frailty and fall risk. It performed best for MCI; with improvement for frailty and fall risk, recalibration, and external validation, such a model could support efficient screening of older adults for several conditions at once. KEYWORDS mild cognitive impairment; frailty; fall risk; machine learning; multi-label classification; classifier chain; gait; dual task; explainable artificial intelligence; Shapley additive explanations.

papers.title: The ITE-Transformer: A pre-trained foundation model for predicting individualized treatment effects from electronic health records
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.26368479 v1

summary.background:
- Electronic health records (EHRs): routine clinical databases of diagnoses, prescriptions and visits.
- Foundation model: a large model first trained on broad data with no specific task in mind, then reused for particular tasks.
- Transformer: a neural network architecture, widely used in language models, that processes sequences such as a patient's history of events.
- Self-supervised pre-training: learning from the data's own structure (for example, predicting hidden parts of a record) without manual labels.
- Individualized treatment effect (ITE): an estimate of how much one specific patient's outcome would change under one treatment versus another; it cannot be observed directly, since each patient receives only one treatment.
- Doubly robust estimation: a causal method that stays reliable if either of two underlying models (treatment or outcome) is reasonably correct.
- Comparative effectiveness: research comparing two existing treatments in routine practice.
- Discrimination and calibration: how well a model ranks patients by risk, and how closely its predicted probabilities match observed rates.
- All of Us Research Program: a large US research cohort with linked health data.
summary.one_liner: A transformer-based foundation model, pre-trained with self-supervision on longitudinal EHR diagnosis and medication histories and combined with doubly robust causal learning, is proposed to estimate individualized treatment effects in two comparative-effectiveness tasks using All of Us data.
summary.plain: This paper asks how a patient's health outcome might differ depending on which treatment they receive, using years of patient records from electronic health systems. The authors built a model that first learns general patterns from patients' diagnosis and medication histories, then estimates treatment effects for individuals. They tested it on two comparisons: diabetes drugs (GLP-1 agonists versus DPP-4 inhibitors) and cancer treatments (immunotherapy versus chemotherapy).
summary.why: The text reports that the model predicted treatment assignment and outcomes somewhat better than standard tabular machine learning and a transformer without pre-training, and that it found varying predicted effects across patients. Whether this improves real-world evidence generation depends on validation the summary does not describe, such as evaluation against randomized trial results.

papers.abstract: Transformer-based foundation models have shown strong potential for modeling longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs), yet existing models focus primarily on risk prediction rather than treatment effect estimation, which limits evidence generation. Here, we introduce the ITE-Transformer, a transformer-based framework that combines self-supervised representation learning from longitudinal patient trajectories with doubly robust causal machine learning for predicting individualized treatment effects (ITEs). As a result, our ITE-Transformer allows to study counterfactual questions of how an individual patient's outcome may differ under alternative treatment strategies. The ITE-Transformer learns temporally contextualized representations of patients' diagnosis and medication histories and subsequently uses these representations to predict treatment assignment, treatment-specific outcome risks, and patient-specific ITEs. The ITE-Transformer is trained using structured EHR data from ~350,000 participants in the All of Us Research Program and evaluated in two clinically different comparative-effectiveness tasks: (i) GLP-1 receptor agonists versus DPP-4 inhibitors among patients with type 2 diabetes, with major adverse cardiovascular events as the outcome, and (ii) immunotherapy versus chemotherapy in a pan-cancer cohort, with all-cause mortality as the outcome. Across both applications, the ITE-Transformer improves the discrimination and calibration of treatment assignment and outcome models compared with existing tabular machine learning approaches and an otherwise identical transformer trained without self-supervised pre-training. The ITE-Transformer further identifies substantial heterogeneity in predicted ITEs and yields interpretable patterns of treatment response associated with patients' diagnoses, medication histories, and comorbidities. Together, our work demonstrates how clinical foundation models can be developed for analyzing heterogeneity in treatment effects and thus support real-world evidence generation.

papers.title: Automated Screening for Generalized Anxiety Disorder Using Voice Analysis and Machine Learning
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.26367837 v1

summary.background:
- Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD): persistent, excessive worry; screened here with the GAD-7, a 7-item questionnaire where a score of 5 or more was treated as "elevated" symptoms.
- Acoustic features: measurable properties of sound such as pitch (fundamental frequency), loudness and timing; the eGeMAPS set is a standard compact list of these.
- Machine learning classifier: a model that learns from labelled examples to sort new cases into groups (here, elevated vs not elevated).
- AUC-ROC: a 0.5 score means chance-level sorting and 1.0 means perfect; the best acoustic-only model reached 0.594, and the best context-augmented model 0.699.
- Nested cross-validation: a way of testing models on data held out from training, repeated to reduce over-optimistic results; "participant-separated" means no person appears in both training and test sets.
- SHAP: a method that estimates how much each input feature pushes a model's prediction up or down.
summary.one_liner: Machine-learning classifiers trained on acoustic features of neutral read speech, with and without demographic and health context, were evaluated for screening elevated GAD-7 anxiety scores in 1,788 adults from four African countries under participant-separated nested cross-validation.
summary.plain: Researchers asked whether a short recording of someone reading text aloud could help flag possible generalized anxiety. They analysed voice recordings from 1,788 adults in Botswana, Ghana, Nigeria and Tanzania, collected remotely, and compared nine computer models. Voice features alone gave weak results, while adding simple personal information such as health status and age helped more.
summary.why: Remote, low-cost screening could matter in places with few mental health clinicians, but this study reports only modest performance and the authors themselves say external validation is needed. It is a useful check on how far voice alone can go, not evidence that voice screening is ready for use.

papers.abstract: This study evaluated machine learning models for screening elevated generalized anxiety symptoms from remotely collected neutral read speech in 1,788 adults from Botswana, Ghana, Nigeria, and Tanzania. Elevated symptoms were defined by Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item (GAD-7) questionnaire scores [≥] 5. Nine classifiers were assessed across nine scenarios defined by speech-task configuration (short sentence, long passage, or both tasks) and sex stratification under participant-separated, repeated nested cross-validation (CV). Acoustic-only models used the extended Geneva Minimalistic Acoustic Parameter Set, and context-augmented models added age, self-reported health, and sex where applicable. With feature selection, the highest mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCROC) was 0.594 for acoustic-only models and 0.699 for context-augmented models, the latter in the female-only combined-task scenario. Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) identified fundamental frequency descriptors as prominent acoustic predictors, while health status and age were the leading predictors in context-augmented models. Performance varied across scenarios, and feature selection provided no consistent benefit. Secondary regression poorly estimated continuous symptom severity. These findings indicate limited discrimination from neutral speech acoustics alone and improved performance with participant context, warranting external validation.

papers.title: The Shrinking Grace Period and the Downsizing of Ransomware Victims: Exploitation Timelines and Breach Size Among US Health Care Providers, 2016-2026
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.26368300 v1

summary.background:
- CVE: a public identifier for a specific software vulnerability, with a publication date.
- CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog: a US government list of flaws confirmed to be used in real attacks; the paper uses its 1,748 entries.
- Time to exploitation: days between public disclosure of a flaw and its first confirmed use in attacks. A median of 0 days means many were exploited on or before the day they were announced.
- HHS Office for Civil Rights breach portal: US federal reports of health data breaches affecting 500 or more people; the paper analyzes 8,029 reports.
- Hacking/IT incident: the category of breach caused by an outside attack or IT failure, as opposed to theft of paper records or internal misuse.
- Trend test (P value): a statistical check of whether a change over time is likely to be real; P = .40 means no clear further change, while P < .001 means a very unlikely chance result.
- Patching: installing software updates that fix known flaws.
summary.one_liner: A retrospective analysis of CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and HHS breach reports examines how fast software flaws are exploited after disclosure and how the size of hacking breaches at US health care providers changed from 2016 to 2026.
summary.plain: Software flaws are often announced publicly before criminals start using them, and this paper asks how long that gap has been. It also checks whether hacks on US health care providers, as reported to federal regulators, have been getting bigger or smaller over time. The authors found the gap shrank to a median of about a week by 2023-2025, and that the share of provider hacks affecting fewer than 5,000 people rose from 32% in 2022 to 46% in 2025.
summary.why: The findings suggest that small clinics may be hit by attacks that quickly follow public disclosure of a flaw, which bears on how much a patching-based defense can protect them. The text does not show what caused either trend, so the link to generative AI in the conclusions is the authors' suggestion rather than something the data establish.

papers.abstract: Objectives: To examine how quickly software vulnerabilities are exploited after public disclosure, and whether hacking breaches at US health care providers changed in size after 2021, a period in which earlier studies had found attacks concentrating on large organizations. Methods: Retrospective analysis of public data. We linked the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog (1,748 entries) with CVE publication dates to measure time to confirmed exploitation by half-year of publication (2021-2025). We also analyzed 8,029 breach reports submitted to the HHS Office for Civil Rights, focusing on hacking/IT incidents at health care providers. Results: Median time to confirmed exploitation was 24 days for vulnerabilities published from late 2021 to mid 2022, 0 days for those published in the second half of 2022, and 6 days in 2023-2025, with no further shortening across 2023-2025 (P = .40). About a quarter were exploited on or before the day of disclosure. Among provider hacking breaches, the share affecting fewer than 5,000 people fell from 42% in 2016 to 32% in 2022 (trend P = .004) and rose to 46% in 2025 (P < .001). Conclusions: The window between disclosure and exploitation had narrowed to about a week before generative AI was widely available. After 2022, breaches moved toward smaller events, reversing the earlier concentration on large organizations. Defenses that depend on patching speed will not protect small providers.

papers.title: Patient-Expressed Needs, Burdens and Barriers in Taiwanese Online Health Discussions: A Taiwan-Contextualized Friction Framework Applied With Large Language Model-Based Social Listening
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.26365957 v1

summary.background:
- "Social listening" means systematically reading public online posts to learn what people experience.
- "Patient-focused drug development" is a regulatory approach that gathers patients' own views of their conditions and treatments.
- A "large language model" is an AI system trained on text that can label or summarise written material; here it was used as a reader and coder.
- "PTT" is a large Taiwanese forum; "ask-a-physician" services let users submit health questions to doctors.
- A "keyword pipeline" is an automated filter that flags posts containing certain words, a simpler method than reading the full text.
- Agreement checks used a second AI vendor and two physicians' independent labels on 160 posts.
- Taiwan's National Health Insurance is the public system that frames many of the cost and access questions.
summary.one_liner: A large language model was used to read full Traditional Chinese posts from Taiwan's PTT forum and physician Q&A services and code them into eight patient-friction domains, with checks against a second model, physician labels and a keyword pipeline.
summary.plain: Patients and their families often describe struggles online, such as not understanding a diagnosis, feeling distressed, or not knowing where to go, that rarely come up in a doctor's visit. This study read about 10,000 Taiwanese online health posts and questions with an AI language model, sorting them into eight kinds of difficulty. The most common concern was not understanding their condition, followed by emotional strain; family members more often wrote about navigating the system and access problems.
summary.why: It offers a way to hear patient and family concerns at scale, which regulators already recognise as a possible source of patient experience data. The paper also reports that a common keyword-based method missed or distorted several categories, which matters for anyone building similar monitoring tools; its usefulness for actual services still needs testing, as the authors themselves note.

papers.abstract: Background: Patients' difficulties with illness and care (not understanding a result, distress, daily restrictions, not knowing where to go, family strain) may not surface in clinical encounters or records. Regulatory guidance on patient-focused drug development recognizes social-media listening as a source of patient experience data, but no systematic framework exists for Traditional Chinese discussions in Taiwan, and keyword pipelines measure such content poorly. Objective: To characterize patient-expressed needs, burdens and barriers ("frictions") in Taiwanese online health discussions with an eight-domain, Taiwan-contextualized framework, identify whose frictions they are, and assess how securely each is measured. Methods: From a 13.6-million-unit archive of the PTT forum and three ask-a-physician services, seeded samples of 9,131 pipeline-flagged units and 1,000 unflagged forum articles (10,130 distinct units) were read in full by a large language model under rubrics for relevance, author (patient or family member) and eight domains: information gap, emotional burden, lifestyle burden, medication experience, system navigation, access barrier, caregiver burden and cost burden. Profiles were reported separately for forum articles and physician submissions and checked against a second vendor, two physicians' independent labels of 160 accepted and rejected units, and the archive's keyword pipeline. Results: Among 2,395 model-confirmed forum articles, 83.1% voiced at least one friction: information gap 59.5% (physicians 86%-93%), emotional burden 39.0%, medication experience 24.1%, lifestyle burden 22.2% and system navigation 16.3%; access barrier, caregiver burden and cost burden were each below 7%. Of 3,105 submissions, nearly all were questions and 53.8% also carried a burden. Navigation rarely concerned insurance (9.1%). Family-authored forum articles (14.5%) more often voiced emotional burden (54.9% vs 36.3%), navigation (34.8% vs 13.2%; instrument-dependent) and access barriers (16.4% vs 4.7%), and patient-authored articles lifestyle burden (24.8% vs 6.9%); caregiver burden came with emotional burden in 86.0% of articles voicing it. Emotional and lifestyle burden were commoner in forum articles than submissions under the model, a second vendor and both physicians; medication experience and navigation were instrument-dependent, and physicians disagreed on cost (32% vs 4%). The keyword pipeline had stored its information-gap output for 29.9% of model-confirmed reference-stratum units and over-counted insurance navigation 2.9-fold; its relevance flag was 50.5% precise for forum articles and reached an estimated 42.9% of patient-voice articles. Conclusions: Systematic listening organized Taiwanese patients' and families' online accounts into eight clinically interpretable friction domains, led by the need to understand and by emotional burden, with family-authored posts more often voicing navigation and access difficulty. These expressed concerns may not surface in routine encounters; they identify candidate targets for patient-centred communication and services, which require evaluation. Some domain levels depended on the reader, and keyword pipelines missed or distorted them, so such work needs full-text reading, explicit definitions and clinician checks. Keywords: social media; patient experience data; patient-focused drug development; unmet needs; caregivers; natural language processing; large language models; content analysis; Taiwan; national health insurance

papers.title: Uncertainty-aware longitudinal prediction of multiple adverse pregnancy outcomes
authors: van der Hout-van der Jagt, M. B.
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.15.26368140 v1

summary.background:
- Antenatal care: prenatal check-ups where risk is reassessed at several gestational-age windows (visits 1 to 3 here).
- Logistic regression: a standard statistical model that turns risk factors into a probability of an outcome.
- Conformal prediction: a method that wraps any model and returns a set of possible answers guaranteed to contain the truth at a chosen rate (here 90%); when the set holds both answers, the case is flagged for review.
- Mondrian conformal prediction: a variant that applies this guarantee separately within subgroups, here likely by outcome class.
- Coverage: the share of cases where the returned answer set includes the true outcome.
- nuMoM2b: a US cohort of nulliparous (first-time) pregnant women, 2010 to 2013.
- Fetal growth restriction and large for gestational age: abnormal fetal size relative to gestational age.
- Adjusted difference: a comparison between groups after statistically accounting for other factors; a confidence interval spanning zero means the result is not clearly different from no effect.
summary.one_liner: Secondary analysis of the nuMoM2b cohort testing whether a woman's trajectory of repeated logistic-regression risk predictions, and Mondrian conformal prediction sets with a "review" option, add information for five adverse pregnancy outcomes across three antenatal visits.
summary.plain: Doctors reassess a pregnant woman's risk of complications such as gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, and abnormal fetal growth at several prenatal visits. This study asks two things: whether a woman's earlier risk estimates tell us anything beyond her latest one, and whether a method that can answer "low risk", "high risk", or "needs review" stays reliable across repeated visits. The authors report that for fetal growth outcomes, women whose risk rose to high only recently showed somewhat higher outcome rates than those high-risk at every visit, though the confidence intervals include zero, and that reliability was close to target at each single visit but lower when all three visits were considered together.
summary.why: Most prenatal risk tools give one prediction at one point in time and force a yes or no answer, so this work looks at how risk changes over pregnancy and how much uncertainty is admitted. It may matter for designing repeated-use clinical tools, though the evidence is from one cohort with wide uncertainty, so its clinical value is not yet established.

papers.abstract: BackgroundRisk of pregnancy complications is reassessed at each antenatal visit, but whether earlier predictions add information beyond the most recent one is unclear. Classifying every prediction as low or high risk can leave uncertainty unexpressed. Whether reliability per visit holds across visits is also unclear. MethodsThis secondary analysis included 9,289 nulliparous women from the nuMoM2b cohort (eight US centres, 2010-13). Logistic regression models predicted gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, suspected fetal growth restriction and large for gestational age at 6-13, 16-21 and 22-29 weeks (Visits 1-3). Mondrian conformal prediction reported no (low risk), yes (high risk), or both (review). To test whether prediction history adds information beyond the Visit 3 prediction, we compared, among women classified as high risk at Visit 3, those first classified as high risk at Visit 2 or 3 (emerging high) with those classified as high risk at all three visits (persistent high), adjusting for Visit 3 predicted probability. FindingsThe adjusted proportion with the outcome was higher in the emerging-high than the persistent-high group, by 6.1 percentage points for large for gestational age (95% CI -0.4 to 12.2) and 3.8 percentage points for suspected fetal growth restriction (-0.9 to 8.1). Other outcomes showed adjusted differences close to zero. With conformal prediction calibrated to a 90% level at each visit, the reported answers included the actual outcome in 89.6-90.6% of women at each visit (coverage). Coverage decreased when each womans three visits were considered together (79.0-85.4%). InterpretationFor fetal growth outcomes, how a womans predicted risk evolved during pregnancy may add information beyond her Visit 3 prediction. For repeated clinical use, the target coverage level should reflect the acceptable risk of incorrect low- or high-risk classifications over a womans follow-up and the clinical decisions supported at each visit. FundingNone. Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSWe searched PubMed from database inception to Oct 28, 2026, for English-language studies in humans, combining terms for gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, fetal growth restriction or small for gestational age, and large for gestational age with terms for prediction models and for longitudinal or repeated assessment, risk trajectories, conformal prediction, or predictive uncertainty. We also searched for conformal prediction applied to longitudinal clinical data. Most models predicted a single complication at a fixed gestational age. Longitudinal models updated risk using repeated measurements of blood pressure, biomarkers or fetal biometry, and some showed that changes in these measurements, including fetal growth velocity, improved prediction. We found no study that tested whether a womans earlier predictions add information beyond her most recent prediction. Individual-level uncertainty was rarely quantified in antenatal prediction, and we found no application of conformal prediction in antenatal care. Conformal methods have been used for repeated prediction in other clinical settings, but we found no evaluation of how often prediction sets include the actual outcome across a patients successive predictions.

papers.title: Evaluation of System One Models on Biomedical Texts
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.15.26368126 v1

summary.one_liner: This paper benchmarks three "System One" models (SOMs) against three general-purpose large language models (LLMs) on seven biomedical datasets, comparing accuracy, inference cost, and confidence-based routing between the two model types.
summary.plain: Researchers asked whether smaller, cheaper AI models designed for fast, intuitive-style answers can handle medical and biomedical text tasks nearly as well as large general-purpose AI models. They tested both kinds on question answering, error detection, data extraction, and clinical-note assessment. The most capable large model scored highest on every task, while the strongest cheaper model was competitive and cost under 1% of that large model on most datasets.
summary.why:
The work points to a practical trade-off: cheaper models may be good enough for many predefined-choice biomedical tasks, and routing easy cases to them could cut costs. The text itself notes the findings still need evaluation on closed (held-out, non-public) datasets, so the advantages should be treated as preliminary.</why>
<parameter name="background">- Large language model (LLM): a general-purpose AI system trained on huge amounts of text, used here as the comparison baseline.
- "System One" model (SOM): the paper's term for a model class; the abstract does not define its design in detail, so it is unclear from the text how these models work internally.
- Inference cost and latency: the price and time to get an answer from a model.
- Confidence calibration: how well a model's stated confidence matches how often it is actually right.
- Confidence-based routing: sending a query to a cheap model first and passing it to a more powerful model only when confidence is low.
- Cost-matched random referral: a baseline that sends the same share of queries to the bigger model at random, to check whether routing by confidence actually helps.
- Endpoint: a specific task-and-dataset evaluation setting.
- Benchmark accuracy: the share of test items answered correctly.</why>
<parameter name="difficulty">intermediate

papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo compare the performance and cost of System One models (SOMs) with general-purpose large language models (LLMs) on biomedical tasks and evaluate confidence-based routing. Materials and MethodsWe evaluated three SOMs and three LLMs across seven datasets and eight endpoints covering question answering, error detection, structured extraction, and clinical-note assessment. Outcomes included task-specific performance, recorded inference cost and latency, and confidence calibration. Calibration data determined routing schemes and confidence thresholds to evaluate test predictions, with cost-matched random referral as a comparator. ResultsClaude Opus 5.5 had the highest primary performance on all eight endpoints. The strongest SOM, Jev, had competitive performance with the evaluated LLMs and cost less than 1% of Opus on most datasets. Three selected SOM-to-LLM routes reduced costs by 30.0%-71.7% relative to the receiving LLM, with modest reductions in performance. On one benchmark, SOM-to-SOM routing achieved 91.1% accuracy, compared with 82.3% and 82.2% for the individual models. DiscussionSOMs offered favorable performance-cost tradeoffs for most tasks. The magnitude of the advantages depended on task structure and prompting requirements. Confidence-based routing between SOMs and LLMs can leverage complementary model strengths and offers additional flexibility in performance-cost tradeoffs. The price advantages offered by SOMs can facilitate experimentation and development of workflows. This warrants further evaluation on closed datasets. ConclusionFor biomedical tasks with predefined choices, SOMs represent a competitive stand-alone or first-stage approach.

papers.title: Enrollees and Early Lessons from an Agentic Healthcare Platform with Physicians in the Loop
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.12.26367291 v1

summary.background:
- Agentic AI platform: software where a large language model (a text-generating AI) carries out multi-step tasks for a user, here with physicians reviewing its work.
- Physician escalation: the AI passing a case to a human doctor.
- Laboratory orders: requests for blood or other lab tests.
- Functional or symptom-defined disorders: conditions diagnosed mainly by symptoms, such as irritable bowel syndrome or chronic fatigue, without a clear structural cause.
- Care fragmentation: when a patient's outpatient care is spread across many different providers, here measured with a threshold for "high" fragmentation.
- National Health Interview Survey (NHIS): a large annual US government survey used as the comparison benchmark.
- Percentage points: the absolute difference between two percentages.
- Direct-to-consumer telemedicine: online medical services that patients access directly, without a referral.
summary.one_liner: A descriptive study of 3,223 enrollees in Lotus AI, a free, physician-supervised agentic healthcare platform, comparing their chronic disease burden, care fragmentation, and functional-disorder utilization against national survey benchmarks.
summary.plain: This paper looks at who signs up for an AI health assistant that works alongside doctors. The authors examined 3,223 people who joined the free Lotus AI platform between February and July 2026 and compared them with national health survey figures. The users were middle-aged (median age 51), mostly male, and had more chronic conditions than national averages in each age group.
summary.why: Most published data on digital health users comes from younger, mostly female telemedicine patients, so a different user profile matters for how such tools should be designed. The paper argues that AI care platforms should check their users against national benchmarks early; its practical impact depends on how far these findings generalize beyond this one platform, which the text does not establish.

papers.abstract: Agentic healthcare platforms that combine large language models with physician oversight are growing quickly, but little is known about who uses them. We characterized 3,223 enrollees of Lotus AI, a free, physician-supervised agentic platform, who completed onboarding, messaged the agent, and had a linked health record between February and July 2026, and compared them with national benchmarks. Median age was 51 years and 62% were male. Chronic condition prevalence exceeded 2024 National Health Interview Survey estimates in every age band by 4 to 7 percentage points; 18% had a functional or symptom-defined disorder; among the 30% with four or more ambulatory visits in the prior year, care was spread across nearly five providers, with 44% meeting a threshold for high fragmentation. Users with functional disorders generated 1.8 times as many physician escalations and 2.6 times as many laboratory orders as other users, but no more prescriptions. This profile differs from the younger, predominantly female populations reported for direct-to-consumer telemedicine. It moves chronic disease management, functional disorder pathways, and care coordination from aspirations to design requirements, and we argue that deployed AI care platforms should characterize their populations against national benchmarks early.

papers.title: Future-Information Leakage in 30-Day Readmission Prediction: An Empirical Audit and a Calibrated Electronic Health Record Model in Medicare-Insured Adults
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.26368026 v1

summary.background:
- Readmission: a patient returning to hospital soon after discharge; here, within 30 days.
- Medicare: US government health insurance mainly for people aged 65 and over, plus some younger people with disabilities.
- MIMIC-IV: a public, de-identified database of hospital records from an intensive care center in Boston.
- Data leakage: when a model is trained on information that would not be available at the time of prediction, making it look more accurate than it will be in practice.
- AUROC (area under the ROC curve): a 0–1 score for how well a model ranks higher-risk patients above lower-risk ones; 0.5 is chance, 1.0 is perfect.
- Calibration: whether predicted risks match actual observed rates.
- XGBoost: a widely used machine-learning method that builds many decision trees.
- LACE and HOSPITAL: two established, simple readmission risk scores used as comparisons.
- Patient-grouped validation: testing so that the same patient never appears in both training and test data.
- Bootstrap confidence intervals: a resampling method to estimate the uncertainty of a result.
summary.one_liner: A retrospective study of 236,906 Medicare-insured MIMIC-IV admissions that finds a future-information leak inflated a 30-day readmission model's discrimination, and reports a corrected, calibrated XGBoost model with AUROC about 0.706 (internal validation only).
summary.plain: The paper looks at a model that predicts whether a patient will return to the same hospital system within 30 days of going home. The authors found that one history-based input quietly used records from later visits, which made the model look better than it really was. After removing that leak and related problems, the corrected model still predicts somewhat better than chance (AUROC about 0.71), and its predicted risks match observed rates, but it has only been tested internally.
summary.why: Readmission models are used to decide who gets follow-up care, so a hidden leak that makes them look more accurate could mislead hospitals and create false conclusions about groups of patients. The paper's main lesson is that simple empirical checks can catch leaks that documentation audits miss; the authors themselves say external validation is needed before any clinical use.

papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo develop and internally validate a calibrated discharge model of 30-day within-system readmission in Medicare-insured adults, and to quantify how a future-information leak and outcome artifacts distorted performance, timing, and subgroup conclusions. Materials and MethodsRetrospective study of 236,906 Medicare-insured MIMIC-IV v3.1 admissions (87,750 patients; prevalence 21.4%). Predictors were audited for discharge-time availability; history features were tested for future information and recomputed from raw timestamps. A consensus gradient-boosted (XGBoost) model was selected inside patient-grouped folds; CIs used patient-cluster bootstrap. ResultsA feature documented as a prior 180-day length-of-stay trend used each patients whole record, including later admissions; removing it and two derived terms lowered test area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) from 0.774 to 0.706. The corrected procedure reached an out-of-fold AUROC of 0.7057 (95% CI 0.7016 to 0.7102; primary); the 44-feature model scored 0.7056 on the historically exposed test partition (calibration slope 0.99), above reconstructed LACE and HOSPITAL (both P<.001). A day-1 discrimination peak largely reflected 2,368 probable administrative continuations within 1 hour of discharge; merging these into the preceding stay gave test AUROC 0.698 (0.702 after refitting). The White minus Black AUROC difference was 0.003 (95% CI -0.018 to 0.024); specificity was lower for Black patients (0.61 vs 0.69). DiscussionDocumentation audits and patient-grouped validation missed a leak that inflated discrimination and created spurious subgroup and calendar-period differences; simple empirical checks found it. ConclusionEmpirical leakage checks should accompany availability audits. The corrected model is calibrated, moderately discriminating, and needs external validation before clinical use.
